summary: Angela Patel, a feminist and self-described ex-tomboy, reflects on how her gender expression changed from childhood tomboy identity to a more feminine, popularity-driven presentation as a teen. She argues the tomboy label both offered community and reinforced harmful stereotypes and internalized misogyny. The essay contends that rigid gender binaries are socially conditioned from early childhood and urges teaching children respect for gender diversity instead of attaching outdated labels to them.
one_line: Angela Patel reflects on her shift from tomboy to 'girly-girl' and argues that labels like 'tomboy' reinforce a rigid gender binary.
key_facts: Angela Patel wrote 'A Tomboy Story' for FEM, UCLA's feminist newsmagazine, dated February 25, 2020.
The Oxford Dictionary defines a tomboy as 'a girl who enjoys rough, noisy activities traditionally associated with boys.'
Patel says the archetypal tomboy in 20th century literature and pop culture is white, straight and middle class.
Patel describes her tomboy friends as bonding over their 'mutual disgust for princesses, fairies and all things pink.'
Patel says she was embarrassed to check out cheesy YA romance novels from the library, worried it threatened her 'tomboy brand.'
Patel writes that her transition from tomboy to girly-girl was fueled by peer pressure and the bodily changes she experienced as a teen.
Patel says she measured her self-worth with Instagram likes and by comparing herself to the prettiest and most popular girls she knew.
Patel writes that 'We teach young girls to hate themselves in subtle but pervasive ways.'
Patel notes that many tomboys come to identify as queer or trans, but many do not, so the tomboy experience is not one experience.
The essay cites studies in American preschools finding little girls are socialized to be polite, quiet and still, while young boys are given freedom to be loud, curious and even violent.
Patel says gender reveal parties, baby showers and infant fashion display gender and associate preferences with whether a child is designated male or female.
Patel concludes that the idea that some girls are tomboys and some aren't 'needs to be left in the past.'
FEM has been UCLA's feminist newsmagazine since 1973.
